content: Dental plaque is a biofilm, typically clear in color, that accumulates on the surface of teeth. If it is not removed regularly, it can result in the development of dental caries (tooth decay) or periodontal diseases, such as gingivitis. The biofilm is primarily composed of bacteria, with the most common species being Streptococcus mutans and various anaerobic bacteria. The specific bacterial composition of the plaque varies depending on its location within the oral cavity. Examples of anaerobic bacteria found in dental plaque include Fusobacterium and Actinobacteria. The microorganisms present in dental plaque are naturally found in the oral cavity and are generally harmless under normal conditions. However, if plaque is not removed through regular toothbrushing, it can accumulate into a thick layer. In this state, the bacteria closest to the tooth surface shift to anaerobic respiration. During this process, they produce acids that lead to the demineralization of the tooth surface, ultimately causing dental caries. Saliva, which normally helps neutralize acids and remineralize tooth surfaces, cannot penetrate the thickened plaque layer. As a result, it is unable to counteract the acid produced by the bacteria. Over time, the accumulated plaque can also become mineralized, forming dental calculus (tartar). The composition of the microorganisms within the plaque changes as it ages, making older plaque more harmful. For instance, plaque that is 12 hours old is significantly less damaging than plaque that has been left undisturbed for several days. The prevalence of tooth decay has increased significantly in modern times, particularly during the 20th and 21st centuries. In contrast, teeth used for processing a natural diet, such as raw meat and fresh vegetables, were likely to remain intact and functional for a lifetime. Mouthwash, also referred to as mouth rinse, is commonly used as part of oral hygiene practices. Antiseptic and anti-plaque mouth rinses are designed to kill bacteria responsible for plaque formation, gingivitis, and bad breath (halitosis). Additionally, anti-cavity mouthwashes contain fluoride, which helps protect against tooth decay.
